books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by James M. Mason, March 4, 1850

stimulus.source_note: John C. Calhoun, speech on the slavery question, read in the Senate by Senator James M. Mason, March 4, 1850 (Congressional Globe, 31st Congress, 1st session). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
I have, Senators, believed from the first that the agitation of the subject of slavery would, if not prevented by some timely and effective measure, end in disunion.

. . .

You have thus had forced upon you the greatest and the gravest question that can ever come under your consideration: How can the Union be preserved?

. . .

To this question there can be but one answer, — that the immediate cause is the almost universal discontent which pervades all the States composing the Southern section of the Union.

. . .

It is a great mistake to suppose that disunion can be effected by a single blow. The cords which bind these States together in one common Union are far too numerous and powerful for that. Disunion must be the work of time.

. . .

I return to the question with which I commenced, How can the Union be saved? There is but one way by which it can with any certainty; and that is, by a full and final settlement, on the principle of justice, of all the questions at issue between the two sections.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: According to Calhoun, what had endangered the Union?

options.text: The Southern states' almost universal discontent over slavery agitation.
California's request to enter the Union as a free state.
options.misconception: California's admission is part of the crisis, but Calhoun names Southern discontent — not the admission itself — as the immediate cause.

options.text: The election of a president who opposed the compromise.
options.misconception: Background from the books: President Taylor opposed Clay's package, but Calhoun's speech blames the agitation of slavery, not any president, for endangering the Union.
Foreign interference appears nowhere in the speech; Calhoun blames the slavery agitation at home.

rationales.A: Calhoun names the cause directly: “the immediate cause is the almost universal discontent which pervades all the States composing the Southern section of the Union.”
rationales.B: California's admission is part of the crisis, but Calhoun names Southern discontent — not the admission itself — as the immediate cause.
rationales.C: Background from the books: President Taylor opposed Clay's package, but Calhoun's speech blames the agitation of slavery, not any president, for endangering the Union.
rationales.D: Foreign interference appears nowhere in the speech; Calhoun blames the slavery agitation at home.
rationales.general:
1. Find the question Calhoun asks first: what has endangered the Union?
2. Take his answer as he gives it: the immediate cause is Southern discontent, spread across the whole section.
3. Trace that discontent to its root: the agitation of the slavery question, which he has warned about from the first.
Remember: when a speaker names an “immediate cause,” he is telling you what to fix first.
